paras: The attempted lynching of Annie Rodwell was a mob pursuit of a married Black woman in southern Georgia in August 1920, organized, according to the Phoenix Tribune, by the family of N. N. Starling, a married white man who had been seeing her. The couple escaped to Pittsburg, Pennsylvania, where both were jailed while Georgia sought their extradition, a case two Black weeklies presented as revealing Southern race relations.

Both lived at Hahira, Georgia, where Starling's father was a wealthy lumberman and Rodwell's husband worked on the Starling plantation. About two years earlier, the Tribune wrote, the elder Starling organized "a party of lynchers to take the woman away," which his son turned back by claiming the Rodwell house was full of armed Black people. Rodwell then moved to Valdosta, fourteen miles away.

Starling kept visiting her, although he knew "his father and brothers would lynch the colored girl." About two weeks before the Tribune's Aug. 25 dispatch, his family caught him at her house and organized another lynching party. Warned in time, Starling drove Rodwell twelve miles to a swamp, where they spent the night "in water up to their knees hiding from the mob," before taking a train to Pittsburg.

By Aug. 18 the couple were in a Pittsburg jail fighting extradition instituted by Georgia. Starling said he would return without extradition papers but that Rodwell would be lynched if she went back. No report of the extradition's outcome, or of action against the lynching party, appears in the coverage.

No white-press report was found. The Chicago Whip's short Aug. 21 dispatch, headlined "HOLD WHITE MAN AND COLORED WOMAN ON MANN ACT," told "how white men of the south separate colored men from their wives" and did not mention a mob. The Phoenix Tribune's front-page special of Aug. 28, "STRANGEST CASE IN HISTORY OF SOUTH ATTRACTS ATTENTION," supplied the account of the lynching parties and said the case "again shows up racial relations in the South in their true light." Where the Whip led with a charge against the couple, the Tribune centered the danger to Rodwell.
The papers gave Starling's initials as N. L. and N. N., and only the Whip's headline named the Mann Act; both texts otherwise spoke only of extradition by Georgia.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Annie Rodwell
bases: The Phoenix Tribune reports that a 'lynching party' was organized against Mrs. Rodwell, a Black woman, and that she hid overnight from the mob before escaping by train; no one was killed (A2).

No one was killed: the only account of the mob says the couple escaped it (A2). The party was an unlawful band of unstated size organized over a white man's relationship with a Black woman, so this was an attempted lynching, not a completed one (A2).

Two Black papers agree that Starling and Mrs. Rodwell were jailed in Pittsburg while Georgia sought extradition (A1, A2), but only the Phoenix Tribune reports the lynching party and the flight (A2); no white-press report was found.

accounts.label: Tribune special correspondent (Pittsburg)
accounts.gist: Starling's family twice organized lynching parties against Mrs. Rodwell; the second time the couple drove to a swamp, hid overnight and took a train to Pittsburg, and Starling said she would be lynched if returned.

accounts.label: Chicago Whip dispatch (Pittsburg)
accounts.gist: The couple were jailed fighting Georgia extradition; the bill of particulars told how Starling separated Mrs. Rodwell from her husband. No mob is mentioned.

sources.note: Special from Pittsburg, Aug. 25: Starling's family organized two lynching parties against Mrs. Rodwell; second sent the couple fleeing to a swamp and then by train to Pittsburg.
quotes: The case is the strangest that has ever come to light in the history of the local courts and again shows up racial relations in the South in their true light.
Another lynching party was organized, of which Starling learned just in time to get the girl in his automobile and drive twelve miles to a nearby swamp
Starling says he is perfectly willing to go without extradition papers, but he knows if his soulmate goes back, she will be lynched.
